source.title: A Few Problems on Monodromy and Discriminants

accepted.question_text: Let f:(C^n,0)->(C,0) be an isolated holomorphic function singularity with Milnor number μ, let F(x,λ) be its miniversal deformation over C^μ, and let Σ be the complete bifurcation set of parameters for which f_λ has fewer than μ distinct critical values near the origin. The Lyashko-Looijenga map sends λ to the unordered collection of μ critical values. For a non-simple singularity, what are explicit braid-group obstructions to lifting braids in the configuration space of μ critical values to paths in C^μ minus Σ; equivalently, which braids cannot be lifted?
accepted.context_brief: braid obstructions to Lyashko-Looijenga lifting

evidence.quote:
Let f : (Cn, 0) → (C1, 0) be an isolated holo-
morphic function singularity, µ its Milnor number, F (x, λ) : ( Cn ×
Cµ, 0) → (C1, 0) the miniversal deformation of f , and Σ ⊂ Cµ the
complete bifurcation set of functions of this deformation

The Lyashko–Looijenga map sends any point λ from
a small neighborhood Bε of the origin in Cµ to the unordered collection
of critical values of the function fλ at points close to 0 ∈ Cn

Problem 1A: to present explicit obstructions to the Lyashko-Looijenga
covering in the terms of braid groups. Which braids cannot be lifted to
the space Cµ \ Σ?

accepted.question_text: Given a non-simple singularity, a perturbation f_λ with μ different critical values, and an initial Dynkin diagram defined by a distinguished system of non-intersecting paths from 0 to those critical values, which Dynkin graphs can be obtained from the initial diagram by formal Picard-Lefschetz moves associated with a braid but nevertheless cannot occur as Dynkin diagrams of Morsifications with the same critical values and the same path system?
accepted.context_brief: formal versus realizable Dynkin diagrams

evidence.quote:
Given a conﬁguration of µ diﬀerent points z1, . . . , zµ in D \ 0 and a
system of non-intersecting paths connecting them to 0, any pert urba-
tion fλ of f , having these critical values, deﬁnes a Dynkin diagram

Any braid l ∈ π1(B(D, µ)) moves this Dynkin diagram to
another one in accordance with the Picard–Lefschetz formulas

Problem 1B : given a non-simple singularity and a Dynkin diagram
of it deﬁned by an easy distinguished system of paths connect ing 0 to
critical points of fλ, which Dynkin graphs can be achieved from it by

a sequence of formal Picard-Lefschetz moves deﬁned by a brai d, but
cannot appear as Dynkin diagrams of Morsiﬁcations fλ′ with the same
critical values, deﬁned by the same system of paths?

accepted.question_text: For a non-simple singularity, partial collisions of critical values need not be realizable by lifting through the Lyashko-Looijenga submersion in a small parameter neighborhood. Beyond the known obstruction that two vanishing cycles with intersection index ±2 cannot be collided in this way, are there more refined restrictions on critical-value collisions? In particular, if two vanishing cycles have intersection index ±1 or 0, can the collision of their corresponding critical values always be lifted to B_ε via the Lyashko-Looijenga submersion?
accepted.context_brief: refined restrictions on critical-value collisions

evidence.quote:
Then we surely cannot lift to Bε the collision of these two
critical values along these paths (keeping the remaining critical valu es
unmoved).

Problem 1C. Are there more reﬁned restrictions to the collision of
critical values? Is it correct that if the intersection inde x of some two
vanishing cycles is equal to ± 1 or 0, then we can lift the collision of
the corresponding critical values to Bε via the Lyashko–Looijenga sub-
mersion?

accepted.question_text: For an isolated function singularity, how can one give lower bounds for the dimension of its μ-constant stratum in terms of the intersection form of its vanishing cycles? More specifically, when several independent collisions of critical values are prohibited by the vanishing-cycle intersection data, can those prohibited collisions be converted into independent lower-bound directions approaching the μ-constant stratum?
accepted.context_brief: dimension bounds for μ-constant strata

evidence.quote:
In the previous consideration, the existence of two vanishing cycle s
with intersection index ± 2 ensures the non-properness of the Lyashko–
Looijenga map, and hence the fact that the µ = const stratum of the
singularity is positive-dimensional.

Problem 1D. Give more general lower bounds of the dimension of
µ = const strata in the terms of intersection forms of vanishing cycle s.
That is, if we can indicate many independent prohibited collisions of
critical values, then probably the attempt to perform these collisio ns
by the rough force will throw us from the neighborhood of the origin
in Cµ in independent directions (all of which approach the µ = const
stratum).

accepted.question_text: Let f:(C^n,R^n,0)->(C,R,0) be a real function singularity with a real deformation F whose real parameter space R^k is divided into chambers by the real total discriminant of non-Morse functions and functions with critical value 0. For a non-simple real singularity, formal surgeries can be performed on collections of critical values together with their intersection matrix and additional real Morsification invariants, and these formal surgeries can be composed in arbitrary chains. What obstructions determine whether such chains of formal changes are realizable by actual paths in the real parameter space R^k?
accepted.context_brief: real obstructions to chains of formal surgeries

evidence.quote:
The space Rk of real parameters is sepa-
rated into several chambers by the real total discriminant (cons isting
of all non-Morse functions and functions with critical value 0).

For non-simple singularities, we can perform all the same formal
surgeries over the collections of critical values (supplied with the in-
tersection matrix and some additional set of topological invariants of
a real Morsiﬁcation), and combine these formal surgeries in arbitr ary
sequences.
Problem 1E. What are the obstructions to the realization of these
chains of formal changes by paths in the parameter space Rk?

accepted.question_text: For real function singularities of corank 2 and Milnor number μ≤11, an algorithm enumerating chains of formal surgeries reportedly never encountered a formal surgery that could not be realized by a surgery of functions in the versal deformation. Can this experimental realizability observation be proved as a theorem?
accepted.context_brief: theorem-level status of surgery-enumeration experiments

evidence.quote:
An algorithm enumerating all such chains of surgeries was realized
in [18]; at least for singularities of corank 2 and µ ≤ 11 it never met a
formal surgery which could not be realized by a surgery of function s in
the versal deformation.
Can this experimental fact be raised to the theorem level ?

accepted.question_text: Consider a one-parameter family of real analytic functions or polynomials f_τ:(C^n,R^n)->(C,R), for real τ in (-ε,ε), realizing a Morse birth surgery: for τ<0 there are two complex-conjugate critical points, these collide at an A_2 point as τ tends to 0, and then they reappear as two real Morse critical points of neighboring Morse indices. Is there a convenient topological characteristic of f_{-ε} that predicts the integer Morse indices of the two newborn real critical points, not just the parity of the greater index obtained from the sign of an intersection number of conjugate vanishing cycles?
accepted.context_brief: predicting Morse indices after birth surgery

evidence.quote:
Consider an one-parametric family of real analytic
functions (or just polynomials) fτ : ( Cn, Rn) → (C, R), τ ∈ (− ε, ε)
realizing a Morse birth surgery: the functions fτ , τ < 0, have two
complex conjugate critical points which collide in a point of type A2
when τ tends to 0, and after that reappear as two real Morse critical
points of some two neighboring Morse indices.
Problem 1F : is there any convenient topological characteristic of the
function f−ε which allows us to predict these indices?

Then the
sign of their intersection number is well-deﬁned and allows us to guess
the parity of the greater newborn critical point, see [15], [18]. But h ow
can we predict the integer index?

accepted.question_text: In the 6-dimensional real parameter space of pairs of polynomials f_a(x,y)=x^2-y^2+a(x,y) and g_b(x,y)=xy+b(x,y), where a(x,y) and b(x,y) are arbitrary real polynomials of degree at most 1 and the system {f_a=0,g_b=0} always has 2 or 4 real solutions counted with multiplicities, what is the minimal number of open sets covering R^6 such that on each open set there is a continuous map selecting one real solution (x,y) of the system? Since the covering number is at least 2, is the lower bound 2 sharp?
accepted.context_brief: covering number for choosing exact roots of a polynomial system

evidence.quote:
Consider r
the 6-dimensional real space of pairs of polynomials ( fa, gb) : R2 →
R2, where fa(x, y) = x2 − y2 + a(x, y), gb = xy + b(x, y), a(x, y) and
b(x, y) are arbitrary polynomials of degree ≤ 1. Obviously, the system
{fa = 0 , gb = 0 } always has 2 or 4 solutions in R2 (counted with
multiplicities).

Problem 2A. What is the minimal number of open sets Ui covering
R6 such that for any Ui there is a continuous map ϕi : Ui → R2 sending
any pair (a, b) ∈ Ui into some solution of the system (fa, gb)?

The number in question is not less than 2 (indeed, we can emulate the
complex equation z2 = A inside our system, and the covering number
of this equation depending on the complex parameter A is equal to 2).
But is this estimate sharp?

accepted.question_text: For the same 6-dimensional family of real polynomial systems f_a(x,y)=x^2-y^2+a(x,y), g_b(x,y)=xy+b(x,y) with a and b of degree at most 1, what is the corresponding covering-number problem for approximate solution selectors: the continuous map on each open set may choose a point that is merely within a fixed positive ε-neighborhood of some actual root rather than being an exact root?
accepted.context_brief: covering number for approximate root selection

evidence.quote:
Problem 2B. The same questions concerning the approximate solu-
tions. That is, for any i and (a, b) ∈ Ui the value ϕi(a, b) should be not
necessarily a root of (fa, gb), but just a point in the ε–neighborhood of
such a root for some ﬁxed positive ε.

accepted.question_text: For polynomial systems of higher degrees and different numbers of variables, including the already nontrivial case of monic real one-variable polynomials f_a(x)=x^d+a_1x^{d-1}+...+a_{d-1}x+a_d, what are the analogous covering numbers for continuous choices of exact or approximate solutions over parameter spaces?
accepted.context_brief: generalized covering-number questions for polynomial equations

evidence.quote:
These problems have obvious generalizations to polynomial systems
of higher degrees and diﬀerent numbers of variables. They can be n on-
trivial already in the case of polynomials (1) in one real variable, see
[19].

Consider the space Rd of all real polynomials
(1) fa(x) ≡ xd + a1xd−1 + · · ·+ ad−1x + ad, a j ∈ R.

accepted.question_text: Let R^d be the parameter space of monic real degree-d polynomials f_a(x)=x^d+a_1x^{d-1}+...+a_{d-1}x+a_d. Let the essential ramification set be the codimension-2 subvariety of parameters for which f_a has either a real triple root or a pair of complex-conjugate imaginary double roots. Is the complement of this essential ramification set in R^d a K(π,1)-space?
accepted.context_brief: K(pi,1) complement of essential ramification set

evidence.quote:
Consider the space Rd of all real polynomials
(1) fa(x) ≡ xd + a1xd−1 + · · ·+ ad−1x + ad, a j ∈ R.

The essential ramiﬁcation set in the space Rd is the union of all values
a = (a1, . . . , ad) such that the corresponding polynomial fa has either a
real triple root, or a pair of complex conjugate imaginary double roo ts,
see [17]. Obviously, this set is a subvariety of codimension 2 in Rd.
Problem 3. Is its complement a K(π, 1)-space?

accepted.question_text: For a compact domain in R^n, associate to each affine hyperplane the two volumes of the parts into which the hyperplane cuts the domain. In odd dimensions, ellipsoids give algebraic volume functions. Do there exist smooth hypersurfaces in R^n, other than quadrics in odd-dimensional spaces, for which the volume cut from the bounded body by any hyperplane is an algebraic function of the hyperplane?
accepted.context_brief: Arnold's odd-dimensional integrable-ovals problem

evidence.quote:
Any compact domain in Rn deﬁnes a two-valued function on the
space of aﬃne hyperplanes: the volumes of two parts into which the
hyperplane cuts the domain. If n is odd and the domain is bounded
by an ellipsoid, then this function is algebraic

Arnold’s problem (see [2]). Do there exist smooth hypersurfaces in
Rn (other than the quadrics in odd-dimensional spaces ), for which the
volume of the segment cut by any hyperplane from the body boun ded by
them is an algebraic function of the hyperplane?

accepted.question_text: In odd dimension n, non-degenerate parabolic points of the complexification of the boundary, and generic cuspidal edges occurring instead of such parabolic points, obstruct algebraicity of the hyperplane cut-volume function. Are these geometric obstructions sufficient to solve Arnold's problem: must the complexification of every smooth algebraic boundary of degree at least 3 of a compact domain in R^n have a point of one of these obstructing types? If not, can the obstruction list be completed by other singularity types whose occurrence is unavoidable and which also obstruct algebraicity?
accepted.context_brief: sufficiency of parabolic-point and cuspidal-edge obstructions

evidence.quote:
Proposition (see [15]). If n is odd and the volume function deﬁned by
a bounded domain with smooth boundary in Rn is algebraic, then the
complexiﬁcation of this boundary cannot have non-degenera te parabolic
points in Cn.

However, the standard singular points which can occur instead of
parabolic points, the generic cuspidal edges , also prevent the algebraic-
ity of the corresponding volume function, see [15], §III.6.

Problem 4. Are these geometric obstructions suﬃcient to solve the
above problem?
(That is, is it correct that the complexiﬁcation of the smooth alge-
braic boundary of degree ≥ 3 of a compact domain in Rn always has a
point of one of these two obstructing types?) If not, probably we can
complete this list by some other singularity types, also obstructing t he
algebraicity, in such a way that singular points of at least one of thes e
types will be unavoidable on any such hypersurface?

accepted.question_text: Given natural numbers d and N, let P(d;N) be the space of all smooth algebraic hypersurfaces of degree d in R^N. The trivial elements are empty manifolds when d is even and hypersurfaces isotopic to the unknotted R^{N-1} when d is odd. Choose a natural topological complexity measure, such as the total number of homology generators or the minimal number of critical points of Morse functions, whose absolute minimum is attained only on the trivial objects. Can every hypersurface in P(d;N) be connected to a trivial one by a generic path in P(d;N) that undergoes only Morse surgeries, each of which decreases this complexity measure? Equivalently, do there exist nontrivial hypersurfaces for which every surgery increases or at least does not decrease the chosen complexity?
accepted.context_brief: greedy simplification of real algebraic hypersurfaces

evidence.quote:
Given natural numbers d and N, consider the space P (d; N) of all
smooth algebraic hypersurfaces of degree d in RN . The trivial elements
of this space are the empty manifolds if d is even, and the surfaces
isotopic to the unknotted RN −1 if d is odd. Consider also some natural
measure of topological complexity of such hypersurfaces, such a s the
sum of generators of homology groups, or the lowest number of cr itical

Problem 5A. Is it correct that any hypersurface from the space P (d; N)
can be connected with a trivial one by a generic path in this sp ace so
that it experiences only Morse surgeries, any of which decre ases this
complexity measure?
In other words, do there exist non-trivial varieties from ou r space,
any surgery of which increase (or do not change ) this complexity mea-
sure?

accepted.question_text: For smooth algebraic hypersurfaces in P(d;N), replace the purely topological complexity measure by the minimal number of critical points of Morse functions obtained as restrictions of linear functions R^N->R to the hypersurface, and allow both topological surgeries and bifurcations of the dual variety that affect this measure. Does the greedy-simplification question remain true in this setting: can every hypersurface be simplified to a trivial one along a generic path whose relevant surgeries and bifurcations always decrease this linear-Morse complexity?
accepted.context_brief: linear-Morse complexity version of greedy simplification

evidence.quote:
Problem 5B . A version of the previous problem, when the complex-
ity measure is not purely topological: namely, it is the lowe st number
of critical points of Morse functions, deﬁned by restrictio ns of linear
functions RN → R to our varieties. (Correspondingly, the surgeries of
the variety aﬀecting this measure are not only of topologica l nature, but
also include bifurcations of the dual variety ).

accepted.question_text: If greedy simplification of smooth algebraic hypersurfaces in P(d;N) fails, define for each initial topological complexity T the least number F such that every hypersurface of complexity T can be connected to a trivial hypersurface by a generic path in P(d;N) whose intermediate hypersurfaces all have complexity at most F. What upper bound can be given for the function T->F?
accepted.context_brief: upper bounds for non-greedy simplification complexity

evidence.quote:
If the answer to the previous questions is negative, we obtain the
functions associating with any value T of topological complexity the
lowest number F such that any surface of complexity T can be con-
nected with a trivial one by such a generic path in the space P (d; N)
that the complexities of all intermediate hypersurfaces do not exc eed
F .
Problem 5C. Give an upper bound for the function T ↦→ F .

accepted.question_text: Let f:(R^n,0)->(R,0) be a function germ with df(0)=0 and finite Milnor number μ(f), and let ρ(f) be the smallest number of real critical points among real Morsifications of f. Is every real Morsification of f connected to a Morsification with exactly ρ(f) real critical points by a generic path in the base of a versal deformation such that every A_2 Morse surgery along the path decreases the number of real critical points?
accepted.context_brief: local greedy simplification of real Morsifications

evidence.quote:
Let f : (Rn, 0) → (R, 0) be a function germ with d f(0) = 0 and ﬁnite
Milnor number µ(f ). Let ρ(f ) be the smallest number of real critical
points of real Morsiﬁcations of f .

Problem 6A . Is it correct that any real Morsiﬁcation of f can be
connected with one of complexity ρ(f ) by a generic path in the base of
a versal deformation in such a way that all Morse surgeries [A2] in this
path only decrease the number of real critical points ?

accepted.question_text: For a real function germ f:(R^n,0)->(R,0) with df(0)=0 and finite Milnor number, let ρ(f) be the smallest number of real critical points in a real Morsification. What can be said about ρ(f), especially about the two lower estimates given by the index of grad f at 0 and by the Smale number of the relative homology group H_*(f^{-1}((−∞,ε]), f^{-1}((−∞,−ε]))? Can these two estimates differ, do they coincide at least for corank-2 functions, can the relative homology group have nontrivial torsion, and is the Smale-number estimate sharp?
accepted.context_brief: lower estimates and sharpness for ρ(f)

evidence.quote: Problem 6B. What can be said about the number ρ(f )?

Two obvious lower estimates of it are a) the index of grad f at 0, and
b) the Smale number of the relative homology group
(2) H∗(f −1((−∞ , ε]), f −1((−∞ , − ε]))
(i.e. the rank of the free part of this group plus twice the minimal
number of generators of its torsion). Of course, the ﬁrst numbe r does
not exceed the second, but can they be diﬀerent? Do they coincide at
least for functions of corank 2 ?
Can the group (2) have a non-trivial torsion? Is the estimate b) of
the number ρ(f ) sharp?

accepted.question_text: For a real function germ f with finite Milnor number μ(f) and a versal deformation, is every connected component of the complement of the discriminant variety guaranteed to contain a Morsification whose all μ(f) critical points are real?
accepted.context_brief: all-real Morsifications in deformation chambers

evidence.quote:
Problem C Is it true that any component of the complement of the
discriminant variety of a versal deformation contains a Mor siﬁcation,
whose all µ(f ) critical points are real?
This is true for all simple singularities: see [15].

accepted.question_text: For the multidimensional Newton method of Shub and Smale, what universal lower estimate can be given for the radius of convergence domains, analogous to the sharp one-dimensional Reshetnyak estimate that for a degree-n polynomial C->C with simple root z_0 and minimal distance d from z_0 to the other roots, the d^(2n−1)-neighborhood of z_0 lies in the convergence domain of Newton iteration?
accepted.context_brief: universal convergence-radius estimates for multidimensional Newton method

evidence.quote:
Consider a polynomial C1 → C1 of degree n and some its simple root
z0. Let d be the minimal distance from this root to all other roots of this
polynomial. According to [10], the d
2n−1-neighborhood of z0 belongs to
its convergence domain, that is, the Newton’s method starting fro m
any point of this neighborhood converges to z0. This estimate cannot
be improved as an universal function in d and n.
Problem 7 . Give similar universal estimate of the radius of conver-
gence domains of the multidimensional Newton ’s method of [12].
